d.title: Five reasons that are really two
d.caption: The usual list has five entries and three of them are consequences. **The knowledge is editable** — a document is a file and the weights are not — and **the source is identifiable**, so an answer can carry a citation a reader can check. Up-to-date information, no retraining and anything about a training cutoff all follow from the first. Reduced hallucination follows from the second and only partly: a model can still misread a document that is right there.

d.title: Recall against k, and the gap between chunk and document
d.caption: Twenty questions with a known answer-bearing chunk in a known document, over 360,000 characters of real technical prose — headings, code blocks and tables, which behaves differently from clean paragraphs. The gap between the two columns is the finding: at k=5, **document recall is 100% and chunk recall is 95%**. The right document is found and the wrong passage from it is returned, which is a chunking problem rather than a retrieval one.

d.title: Reading the per-question table instead of the summary
d.caption: The first run reported 65% at k=1 and 90% at k=5, and the per-question table showed that **two of the twenty "failures" were not retrieval failures at all**. One wanted a passage in `fine-tuning.md` and got a different passage from `fine-tuning.md` — the right document, the wrong chunk. The other had its answer in a document I had labelled wrongly. A summary metric cannot distinguish a retriever that missed from a test set that lied.

nodes.label: Neither is a retriever failure
nodes.sub: and the summary says they are

nodes.label: So always log the rank per question

d.title: k is a context budget, not a quality dial
d.caption: Search itself is cheap and effectively flat in k — embedding the query, scoring 1,187 chunks and sorting takes **11.02 ms** whatever k you ask for. What k buys is **context tokens**, and those are the cost: 90 at k=1 against 737 at k=10. Which reframes §03's table: going from k=5 to k=20 buys the last 5% of chunk recall for roughly four times the context, paid on every request.

d.title: The three mechanisms, with the build and per-request costs measured
d.caption: *RAG for what the model knows, fine-tuning for how it behaves, prompting first* is sound, and the decision is usually settled by two rows rather than by a capability comparison. **Citations exist only in the middle column.** And the last two rows are the measured halves of 4.1 and 4.2: a style transferred from twelve examples, and a fact came back with its relation reversed under rephrasing.

d.title: Two properties that are unique rather than merely better
d.caption: Most of the comparison is a trade. These two are not available at all from the alternatives. **The update path**: 4.2 measured a fact changed in a document taking effect instantly, while the fine-tuned model kept reciting the old value with no prompt able to override it. **The citation**: the system knows which chunk produced the answer, so it can show its work — and nothing in a set of weights can.

nodes.label: A fine-tune keeps the old value

d.title: A mature system uses all three, each for its own job
d.caption: "Complementary" is right and vague. The useful version assigns each mechanism the thing it is actually good at: **fine-tune the behaviour** — the answer format, the citation discipline, saying *that is not in the documentation* instead of guessing, which 4.1 measured transferring from a dozen examples. **Retrieve the content**, because it changes and needs to be citable. **Prompt the specifics** — the user's tier, the conversation so far, anything genuinely per-request.

nodes.label: Retrieve the content
nodes.sub: it changes, and must be citable

nodes.label: Saying 'not in the documentation'
nodes.sub: is a behaviour, not a fact

nodes.label: Which is why it is fine-tuned

d.title: A bi-encoder is what makes search possible; a cross-encoder is what makes it accurate
d.caption: A retrieval model encodes the query and the document **separately** into the same space, so a dot product predicts relevance — and that separation is the whole reason search works, because documents can be embedded once, offline, and a query compared against a million of them. A cross-encoder takes the pair *together* and is far more accurate, because the two texts can attend to each other — and useless for search, since scoring a million documents means a million forward passes. 5.9 uses one as a second stage over a shortlist, which is the only place it fits.

nodes.label: Far more accurate
nodes.sub: the texts attend to each other

d.title: A 30-point recall spread across four reasonable models
d.caption: The result that matters is the spread: **95% down to 65% at k=5** across four models anyone might pick, which is larger than any other single decision in this module except chunking. And it inverts the general leaderboards — `all-mpnet-base-v2` has the higher published ranking and is **last here**, at 65%, for 9.4× the encode time. There is no substitute for measuring on your own corpus.

d.title: Three things to choose on, and one silent failure
d.caption: Recall on **your** corpus comes first and is measured rather than inferred. Encode throughput sets how long a re-index takes — 26.9 s against 251.8 s on 1,200 chunks is the difference between re-indexing on every deploy and treating it as a batch job. And the trap: `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` has a **256-token limit**, roughly 1,000 characters, so a 2,000-character chunk is silently cut in half before it is embedded. The call succeeds and returns a vector.

d.title: Chunking is the one decision that nothing downstream can undo
d.caption: The text is cut, each piece is embedded, and from that moment **the retriever can only return pieces of that shape**. A better metric, a re-ranker or a rewritten query reorders what chunking produced; none of them can produce a passage that was never a chunk. There is a representational argument too: a chunk becomes **one vector**, so every topic, digression and code block inside it is averaged into a single point — too large and the point represents nothing in particular.

nodes.label: And a chunk is one vector

d.title: Overlap: no measurable effect, and double the index
d.caption: Six overlap settings on the same corpus, and recall at k=5 moves between 90% and 100% **without a trend** — 50 is the worst and 100 the best, which is noise on twenty questions rather than a signal. What overlap does reliably is grow the index: at 250 of 500 it holds **2.0× the chunks** and 2.0× the storage and encode cost. On a corpus with real structural seams, the money is better spent on §04.

d.title: Structure-aware splitting: the cleanest win in the module
d.caption: Fixed splitting cuts every N characters regardless of what is there — mid-sentence, mid-table, mid-code-block. Recursive prefers paragraph breaks over line breaks over spaces. Heading-aware uses the document's own structure. The result is **r@1 from 65% to 85% and r@5 to 100%**, for free, by cutting where the author already cut. Note that document recall was 100% for all three: the gain is entirely in returning the right *passage*.

d.title: The question no chunk boundary can reach
d.caption: One question failed at **every configuration in the sweep**: *"Why divide alpha by r?"*, found at rank 15. The passage that answers it calls the term a **"volume knob"** and never uses the word *divide*. The text is correctly cut, correctly embedded and correctly indexed — the query and the answer simply share no vocabulary. That is a query problem, and it is what 5.8 and 5.9 exist to fix.

nodes.label: The chunking is correct
nodes.sub: so is the embedding and the index

d.title: First ask whether you need an index at all
d.caption: Exact search over the whole corpus of this module — 1,187 vectors — takes **1.743 ms for twenty queries**. Flat search is linear, so the question is only where linear stops being acceptable: at 100,000 vectors it is 8.4 ms, which is still nothing beside an LLM call. **An approximate index is a decision for millions of vectors**, and building one at ten thousand adds a recall risk in exchange for microseconds.

d.title: nprobe is the recall dial, and nlist is the wrong one to turn
d.caption: IVF clusters the vectors at build time and searches only the nearest `nprobe` clusters — so **if the answer is in a cluster you did not probe, you miss it**. At nlist=256, nprobe=1 gives 73% recall for 1.9 ms; nprobe=8 gives **99% for 10.6 ms**, which is the setting to use. Raising nlist to 1024 costs 6× the build time and gives *worse* recall at the same nprobe, because each cluster is smaller so eight of them cover less ground.

d.title: What the index itself costs, which is less than the vectors
d.caption: At 384 dimensions the vectors are 1,536 bytes each and dominate everything. IVF adds **8 bytes** for a list id — 0.5% — and HNSW adds the graph: about 128 bytes at M=16 and 256 at M=32, so **8% and 17%**. Which settles a question people worry about in the wrong order: the index structure is not what makes a vector store large, the embedding dimension is.

d.title: Five stores, and what each one actually is
d.caption: The first row is the clarification that saves the most time: **FAISS is a library, not a service** — in-process, with no persistence or filtering of its own — so comparing it to a vector database is a category error. And the third row is the recommendation most teams should take and do not: **if you already run Postgres**, pgvector gives you transactions, backups and joins to your real data with no new system to operate.
cells: it fits one process and you handle persistence
you would rather pay than operate

d.title: Three metrics, one ordering
d.caption: If every vector has length 1 the relationships collapse. Cosine is the dot product divided by two magnitudes that are both 1. Squared Euclidean expands to `2 − 2(a·b)`, so sorting by L2 ascending **is** sorting by dot product descending. Three names, one ordering — confirmed on twenty questions: identical recall at every k and the **same top-1 result 100% of the time**. The debate about which metric to use is, on normalised vectors, not a debate.

d.title: The first attempt measured nothing, because the vectors were not normalised
d.caption: The equivalence in §01 holds **only** on unit vectors, and these were not: norms ran from **1.4315 to 5.6318, a ratio of 3.93×**. With magnitudes varying that much, cosine and dot product are genuinely different rankings and the comparison would have been meaningful — which is why the first run had to be thrown away and rerun with normalisation. The lesson is to print the norms before concluding anything about the metric.

d.title: Magnitude encodes length, at a correlation of -0.85
d.caption: The norms are not noise. **Chunk length against vector norm correlates at −0.8524** — short chunks get long vectors. Which means an unnormalised dot product systematically favours short chunks, and that is a ranking bias nobody chose: it has nothing to do with relevance and everything to do with how many characters happened to fall between two boundaries.

d.title: Four lines, and the exception
d.caption: Normalise at index time so nothing downstream has to remember; normalise the query **the same way**, because doing one side and not the other produces a ranking that is neither cosine nor dot product; then use inner product, now the cheapest and equivalent to all three. The exception is real: some models encode confidence or specificity in magnitude **on purpose** and are trained with an unnormalised objective, and for those, normalising discards information the model intended you to use.

items.label: Normalise at index time
items.desc: so the stored vectors are unit length

items.label: Normalise the query the same way
items.desc: one side only is a real bug, and a silent one

items.label: Then use inner product
items.desc: cheapest, and now equivalent to the other two

items.label: Verify once: print min, median, max norm
items.desc: if they are not 1.0, something is not doing what you think

items.desc: then magnitude is signal, and the model's own metric is right
